title: 5 Best Asphalt Sealers in 2026: Choose by Chemistry, Not Label
h1: The Best Asphalt Sealer, by Chemistry
query: the best asphalt sealer, by chemistry
description: What is actually in an asphalt sealer, how emulsion, coal tar and oil-based formulas differ, how retail pails compare with contractor bulk, and five picks.
dek: What is actually in an asphalt sealer, how emulsion, coal tar and oil-based formulas differ, how retail pails compare with contractor bulk, and five picks.
intro: Every pail of asphalt sealer is a recipe. Learn the ingredients and you can see past the years printed on the front and pick the formula that fits your pavement.

Strip away the marketing and every asphalt sealer comes down to a few ingredients: a binder, a carrier, something to keep them mixed, and optional extras like filler, sand and polymer. The ratio of those ingredients, not the brand or the number of years on the front, decides how a sealer covers, how long it lasts and how it behaves in bad weather. This guide explains the chemistry, how retail pails differ from what contractors spray, and which products sit where on that spectrum.

sections.h: The 5 Best Asphalt Sealers, by Formula

blocks.p: Each pick represents a distinct point on the formulation spectrum, from thin maintenance emulsion to filled, polymer-modified flagship. We chose them from published product information, label specs such as coverage and minimum temperature, availability, and recurring patterns in owner feedback. We have not run our own test plots, and we do not publish invented durability scores.

From a chemistry standpoint, Airport Grade is what a good residential sealer should look like. It starts with a water-based asphalt emulsion, adds mineral filler for body and texture coverage, and adds polymer to make the cured film more flexible and more resistant to tire scuffing. That three-part recipe is similar in principle to what better contractors build in their tanks, except it arrives pre-mixed and ready to use. The practical results that owners commonly report line up with that formulation: good coverage on moderately worn surfaces, a dark and even finish, and fewer early scuff marks than with unmodified emulsions. The filler content means it settles hard in the pail and needs a drill paddle to remix fully. The label calls for warm, dry conditions, typical of the category. If you want one formula that handles most driveways without matching the product closely to the surface, this is it.

Drive-Maxx 1000 sits at the top of Black Jack's lineup, and its formulation reflects that: a water-based asphalt emulsion with filler and polymer, built for a thicker, more durable film than the brand's lower tiers. In chemistry terms, the step up from a basic pail is mostly in solids content and modifiers, which show up as a darker finish, better hiding power over patches, and more resistance to scuffing once cured. Owners commonly comment on the finish quality first. The limitation is the same for any premium retail pail: on very porous, oxidized asphalt, a lot of that extra material is absorbed by the surface, and a mid-priced filled product can achieve similar results for less. Where Drive-Maxx earns its price is on a smoother driveway in good shape, where the product's solids build an even film rather than disappearing into voids. As always, the long-life language on the label describes product tier, not a guaranteed recoat interval.

blocks.p: Jetcoat Premium leans on filler. Its heavy body is designed to sit up on rough asphalt rather than soaking in, which makes it a good match for surfaces where years of weathering have washed out the fine material between stones. Chemically, filler does two jobs: it adds solids that physically close surface texture, and it thickens the film so that UV and traffic have more material to wear through. The tradeoff is workability. Heavily filled sealers drag more under a brush and need careful mixing so the filler is evenly distributed. Owners commonly report that it covers aging driveways more convincingly than thin, cheap pails, which fits the formulation. Before buying, read the label on the specific pail to confirm the binder type. Coal tar products are restricted in several states and many cities, and you should know exactly which chemistry you are applying. For an older driveway on a budget, it is a sensible middle-ground formula.

Henry's filler-sealer is a value-tier asphalt emulsion with moderate filler content. In formulation terms, it carries fewer solids than premium products, which means a thinner cured film per coat. That is not automatically a weakness. On a driveway that was sealed within the last few years and still has a tight surface, a thinner coat refreshes color and water resistance without building excessive thickness, and buildup is a real cause of cracking and peeling on driveways that are sealed too often. Henry has a long history in asphalt-based roof and pavement coatings, and the product behaves the way a well-made value emulsion should. Owners commonly report that it is easy to spread and good value, and that it fades sooner than flagship products. On oxidized, porous asphalt, expect the first coat to soak in and plan for a second. Run the total cost for two coats against a premium product before deciding the cheaper pail is actually cheaper.

Thin Maintenance Emulsion
#5 Best Thin Maintenance Coat
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0FR1QQRK7?tag=sktiger-20&linkCode=ll1)

Gardner's basic blacktop sealer represents the thin end of the emulsion spectrum: a low-solids asphalt emulsion with little or no filler. Chemically, that is a product designed to add a light layer of fresh binder and color, not to fill or rebuild. There is a place for it. Driveways that are sealed on a reasonable two-to-three-year cycle and still have a tight surface do not need heavy filler, and repeatedly adding thick coats is one of the main causes of the cracked, flaking buildup seen on over-maintained driveways. A thin coat restores appearance and water resistance with minimal thickness. The same thinness makes it a poor choice for gray, raveled asphalt, where it soaks in and leaves a patchy finish. Owners commonly report a quick, easy application and a shorter-lived color than heavier products. Match it to a smooth surface between full sealing cycles and it is good value. Use it on a worn surface and you will be buying more pails.
Pros

ul: Thin, low-solids emulsion that adds minimal buildup

blocks.p: Cons

ul: Little filler, so no help on rough or cracked surfaces

blocks.p: The Bottom Line
The right chemistry for a light refresh on smooth asphalt, and the wrong one for anything worn.

Asphalt pavement is roughly 95 percent stone and sand by weight, held together by about 5 percent asphalt binder, the heavy residue left after refining crude oil. That binder is a complex mix of hydrocarbons. Some of its lighter, oily fractions keep it flexible. Over time, sunlight and oxygen react with the binder and those lighter components are lost or chemically altered.

This process is called oxidation, and it makes the binder harder and more brittle. You see it as a color change from black to gray, and you feel it as a harder, less tacky surface on a hot day. Brittle binder cracks more easily under temperature swings and lets go of fine particles between the stones, a condition called raveling. Water then enters through cracks and voids, and in cold climates, freeze-thaw cycles widen them.

A sealer adds a thin sacrificial layer on top of the pavement. That layer absorbs the UV and oxidation that would otherwise attack the binder below, sheds water, and resists chemical damage from fuel and oil drips for a while. It wears and oxidizes in turn, which is why it needs renewing every few years.

Sealer does not rejuvenate the binder below, despite some marketing that implies it. Rejuvenators are a separate class of products used mainly on commercial and municipal pavement. For a home driveway, sealer is protection for a sound surface. For a practical look at whether it is worth doing on your driveway, see our [pros and cons of sealing asphalt](/sealing-asphalt-driveway-pros-and-cons/).

blocks.p: The asphalt emulsion is the default for residential driveways and the base for nearly everything on retail shelves. It uses the same type of binder as the pavement itself, so the two are chemically compatible. Polymer-modified emulsions are simply better-equipped emulsions, and the line between them is fuzzy, since most mid- and top-tier products include some polymer.

Coal tar and oil-based sealers are the two alternatives, and both have shrinking roles. Coal tar is being pushed out by regulation and health concerns. Oil-based products are being squeezed by air-quality rules on solvent content. Both are covered in more detail below.

If you only need the short version for a home driveway: buy a filled asphalt emulsion, preferably polymer-modified, and spend the rest of your effort on prep. Our ranked list of the [best asphalt driveway sealers](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) applies that logic product by product.

sections.h: What Is Inside an Emulsion Pail

blocks.p: Asphalt and water do not mix on their own. An emulsion uses an emulsifying agent and, in sealcoat, fine clay to suspend tiny droplets of asphalt in water. That suspension is what lets a product made from a sticky, heavy petroleum residue be poured, spread with a squeegee and cleaned up with a hose.

When the sealer is spread on the pavement, water evaporates and is partly absorbed by the surface. The asphalt droplets crowd together and coalesce into a continuous film. This is called breaking and curing, and it is why weather matters so much: cold, humid or rainy conditions slow evaporation and can stop the film from forming properly. It is also why frozen sealer is ruined, since freezing breaks the emulsion in the pail.

Beyond the basic emulsion, products differ in three main ingredients. **Mineral filler** adds body and solids, helping the film cover texture and resist wear. **Sand or aggregate** adds traction and thickness and is standard in contractor mixes. **Polymer**, typically latex or acrylic, makes the cured film more flexible, more resistant to scuffing and less prone to early cracking.

Some products also add natural asphalt such as gilsonite, a hard, naturally occurring bitumen that can contribute to color and hardness. You will see it named on some labels. It is one ingredient among several, not a category of its own, and its presence alone does not tell you whether the overall product is good.

Coal tar sealers use refined coal tar pitch, a byproduct of turning coal into coke for steelmaking. Coal tar resists petroleum solvents better than asphalt does, which is why it became the standard on gas station aprons, parking lots and other places with heavy fuel and oil drips. It also tends to keep a darker color for longer.

The problem is polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, a group of compounds that includes several known or suspected carcinogens. U.S. Geological Survey research has reported PAH levels in coal tar sealcoat on the order of a thousand times higher than in asphalt-based sealcoat, and has linked coal tar sealed pavement to elevated PAHs in nearby house dust and stream sediment as the coating wears off.
WHERE IT STANDS
Washington, Minnesota and many local governments restrict coal tar sealers.

Rules differ by location and change over time, so check your state, county and city before buying any product labeled coal tar or refined tar. Even where legal, it causes strong odor and can irritate skin and eyes during application, especially in sun.

For a home driveway, the case for coal tar is weak. Fuel resistance matters little when the main exposure is an occasional drip from a parked car, and an oil spot primer handles known problem areas. A good asphalt emulsion gives comparable everyday protection without the health, environmental and legal baggage. If a contractor offers a coal tar product, ask for an asphalt-based alternative.

Oil-based sealers, also called cutbacks, dissolve asphalt in a petroleum solvent instead of suspending it in water. When applied, the solvent evaporates and leaves the asphalt behind. Because the solvent thins the asphalt so effectively, these products soak into dry, aged pavement rather than sitting on top as a film.

That penetration is the main argument for them. Some owners of very old, dry driveways like the deep, rich look and the way they seem to soften the surface. Oil-based products can also be somewhat more tolerant of cooler temperatures than water-based emulsions, though they still need dry weather and their cure is typically slower.

The downsides are significant. The solvent smells strongly, is flammable, and counts as volatile organic compounds, which air-quality rules in some states and regions limit. The products can soften the surface in a way that makes it more prone to tire marks for a while, and they cannot be applied over a water-based sealer without compatibility problems. Retail availability has dropped as a result.

Our dedicated comparison of [oil-based versus water-based driveway sealer](/oil-based-vs-water-based-driveway-sealer/) covers when the oil-based route still makes sense. For most homeowners, a filled water-based emulsion is easier, safer and more widely available.

The sealer a professional sprays on your driveway and the pail on a store shelf can start from similar chemistry but end up quite different. Contractors buy bulk concentrate from paving suppliers and build their mix on site, following the manufacturer's mix design. Retail pails arrive ready to use, already diluted and often pre-filled.

blocks.p: The bulk advantage is flexibility. A crew can add sand for traction and thickness, mix in a polymer additive, and adjust dilution to the job. The bulk disadvantage is that quality depends on the person mixing. Over-diluting stretches profit and produces a thin, short-lived coat. Retail pails are less flexible but consistent.

When you get quotes, ask which product line they use, whether it is asphalt or coal tar based, how much water they add, whether they add sand and polymer, and how many coats are included. A reputable contractor will answer easily. Be wary of crews selling leftover sealer from a job down the street at a discount, a well-known scam that often involves heavily thinned material. Our guide to [professional asphalt sealcoating](/asphalt-sealcoating/) covers what a good job should include, and our [cost guide](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/) shows typical prices.

**Sand** is the most common contractor additive. Mixed into the sealer, it adds thickness to the film, improves traction, and gives the surface more wear resistance. Too much sand makes the mix hard to apply and can settle unevenly. Too little leaves a slick, thin surface. Mix designs from sealer manufacturers specify a range by gallon of concentrate.

**Polymer and latex additives** improve flexibility, adhesion and resistance to scuffing and wear. They are what move a basic emulsion into the premium tier. In retail products, the polymer is pre-blended. In contractor mixes, it is often added in the tank.
**Fast-dry additives** are used by some contractors to speed up the cure in marginal weather. They help on cooler or humid days but do not replace the need for dry conditions.

What not to add: water beyond what the label allows, which weakens the film; and any additive not designed for asphalt emulsions, which can break the emulsion or cause poor curing. For a homeowner, the simplest path to a well-equipped sealer is buying a retail product that already contains filler and polymer rather than trying to modify a basic pail.

sections.h: How to Read a Sealer Data Sheet

blocks.p: Most manufacturers publish a technical or product data sheet online that tells you far more than the front of the pail. These are the specs worth checking before you buy.
Specs That Matter Most
Coverage
Sq ft per pail, per coat
Min Temp
Air and surface, usually 50°F+
Cure
Hours before foot and vehicle traffic
Binder
Asphalt, coal tar or solvent

**Coverage per pail** is a rough proxy for solids content. Thin products list higher coverage, while filled and polymer-modified products list lower coverage because there is more material in each pail. On oxidized surfaces, expect lower coverage than listed.

**Minimum temperature** tells you how forgiving the product is. Most water-based sealers call for 50 degrees Fahrenheit and rising, with mild nights through the cure. Some premium products ask for 55. Our guide on [what temperature to seal a driveway](/what-temperature-to-seal-driveway/) covers how to time this regionally.

**Cure times** for foot and vehicle traffic indicate how quickly the emulsion breaks and hardens under standard conditions. Allow more time in cool or humid weather. Finally, the **binder type** should be stated clearly. If you cannot tell whether a product is asphalt or coal tar based from the label or data sheet, do not buy it.

sections.h: Choosing a Formula for Your Pavement

blocks.p: **Sound, smooth driveway on a regular sealing cycle:** a thin maintenance emulsion like Gardner or a value-filled product like Henry. You need fresh color and water resistance, not thickness, and avoiding buildup protects you from future cracking and flaking.

**Average driveway, a few years since the last coat:** a filled, polymer-modified emulsion like Latex-ite Airport Grade. This is the best general-purpose chemistry for a home driveway. Choose Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 if the surface is smooth and finish quality is the priority.

**Weathered, porous, gray asphalt:** a heavy-bodied filled product like Jetcoat Premium or Latex-ite Airport Grade, brushed in for the first coat. Our guide to [reviving gray, oxidized blacktop](/blacktop-driveway-sealer/) covers the extra prep and the bucket math for thirsty surfaces.

**Large driveway, parking area or long rural lane:** get contractor quotes. Bulk sealer with sand and polymer, applied properly, can match or beat retail pails on cost and durability at that scale. And if you have concrete as well as asphalt to deal with, our guide to [choosing a driveway sealer by surface](/best-driveway-sealer/) covers the concrete side, where the chemistry is entirely different.
Also Needed for This Job

mistakes: Buying by the years on the label

The three, six or ten printed on the front of a pail is a product tier name, not a promise. Real service life depends on traffic, sun, plows and prep. Compare formulas instead: filler content, polymer, coverage and binder type tell you much more about how the coat will perform.
Mixing chemistries on the same surface

Putting a water-based emulsion over a fresh oil-based coat, or the reverse, risks poor bonding and peeling. If you do not know what was used last time, clean thoroughly, test a small area and wait a day before committing. When in doubt, stay with water-based asphalt emulsion, which is the most widely compatible choice.

Freezing breaks an emulsion. The asphalt droplets clump together and the sealer will not remix into a smooth, usable liquid, no matter how long you stir. Store pails above freezing over winter, and inspect any pail that spent the cold season in an unheated garage or shed before you use it.
Adding water to stretch the sealer

Extra water reduces the solids per square foot and leaves a thinner, weaker film that wears through sooner. Most retail labels prohibit dilution. If the sealer is too thick to spread, mist the pavement lightly or use a brush. With contractor mixes, ask how much water they add.
Assuming coal tar is the premium option

Coal tar resists fuel better, which is why it was long the commercial standard, but that is not the same as better for a home. It carries significant health and environmental concerns and is restricted in many places. A good polymer-modified asphalt emulsion gives comparable protection for typical driveway use without those drawbacks.
bottomLine: The best asphalt sealer for most homes is a filled, polymer-modified asphalt emulsion. It matches the pavement's own binder, cures with water evaporation, cleans up with a hose and gains real durability from its filler and polymer. Latex-ite Airport Grade is the clearest example, with Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 as the premium alternative and Jetcoat Premium for rougher surfaces. Skip coal tar, treat oil-based products as a niche, and read the data sheet rather than the years on the front of the pail. If you hire a contractor, ask what is in their tank. Chemistry decides how a sealer performs, but prep, weather and two thin coats decide whether that chemistry gets a chance to work.

faqs.q: What is the best type of asphalt sealer for a home driveway?
faqs.a: A filled, polymer-modified asphalt emulsion. It uses the same type of binder as the pavement, cleans up with water, has low odor and gains flexibility and scuff resistance from the polymer. Latex-ite Airport Grade is a good example. Coal tar and oil-based products have niche advantages but significant drawbacks for most homeowners.

faqs.q: What does polymer-modified mean on a sealer label?
faqs.a: It means a polymer, usually latex or acrylic, has been blended into the asphalt emulsion. The polymer makes the cured film more flexible and more resistant to scuffing, cracking and wear. Most mid- and top-tier retail sealers include some polymer, and contractors often add it in the tank. It is one of the main differences between budget and premium products.

faqs.q: Is professional sealcoat better than store-bought sealer?
faqs.a: It can be, but it depends on the contractor. Bulk sealer mixed with sand and polymer at the right dilution is a strong product. Over-diluted bulk sealer is worse than a decent retail pail. Ask what product they use, how much water they add, and whether sand and polymer go into the mix. Reputable crews answer those questions easily.

faqs.q: Why is coal tar sealer banned in some places?
faqs.a: Because of its high content of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. U.S. Geological Survey research has linked coal tar sealcoat to elevated levels of these compounds in house dust and stream sediment as the coating wears. Washington, Minnesota and many local governments have restricted it. It also causes strong odor and skin and eye irritation during application.

faqs.q: Do asphalt sealers rejuvenate old pavement?
faqs.a: No. A sealer adds a protective layer on top of the pavement, restoring color and shedding water, but it does not chemically restore the oxidized binder underneath. Rejuvenators, a separate product class used mostly on commercial and municipal pavement, are designed to penetrate and soften aged binder. For a home driveway, sealing protects what you have rather than reversing aging.

faqs.q: What does sand do in asphalt sealer?
faqs.a: Sand adds thickness and texture to the cured film, which improves traction and wear resistance. Contractors usually add it to bulk sealer according to the manufacturer's mix design. Some retail pails include fine sand or filler already. Too much sand makes sealer hard to spread and can settle unevenly, so follow the product's specified range.

faqs.q: How can I tell what chemistry a sealer uses?
faqs.a: Check the label and the manufacturer's technical data sheet, which should state whether the binder is asphalt emulsion, coal tar or solvent-based. Water cleanup instructions usually indicate an emulsion. A strong solvent smell and instructions to clean up with mineral spirits indicate an oil-based product. If the binder type is not stated clearly, choose a different product.
